And by the way, if you look in the participants, you'll notice a participant named DP: that's our assistant.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin

turns.speaker: Speaker unclear
turns.text: It's not in the chat.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: It should be. I saw it earlier telling us to mute our mics. Oh, it's sending me a message. Okay. Well, let's go forward, and I'd love to get your feedback at the end. This is the first of the four DP listening experiments; last week's was the first session, so this is the second. We have four proposed sessions where we're doing an experiment to understand how we can better govern the DPs through a process of voting, which many of you, maybe all of you, took part in this time. Like I said, we'll do a short recording and would love to get your feedback, so let's jump directly into that.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: I'd like to talk a little bit about gates and where they began. For most of history, a gate was a physical thing: a gap in a wall and someone deciding who passes. The great gates of Babylon, a farm gate, a border crossing. A gate is a decision point: yes or no. In 1937, a young engineer named Claude Shannon showed that electrical switches could make those yes-or-no decisions as logic. A decade later came the transistor. Today, billions of tiny gates open and close every second inside every device you own. Everything digital rests on gates. Video games made gates visible. A door stays locked until you find the key. A level stays closed until you've earned it. In code, gates are everywhere: a login, a permission, a paywall, the filter that decides what lands in your feed. In this series, when I say gates, I mean these digital gates, the ones that decide who or what comes into or goes out of your digital life. And most of them were built by someone else, for their purposes, not yours.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: There are four types of gates we're going to think about. Gates for who can come in: who can join. Gates for what can come in: what content reaches you. Gates for who can leave: can you leave with your identity and history? And the fourth is a what gate: what data can leave.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Who comes in? That's the entrance. Who gets to join the space, a group, a conversation? Who goes out? That's exit. Can you leave and take your identity and your history with you? Most of us only discover this gate when we're trapped behind it. What comes in: everything that reaches you, your feed, your inbox, the comments, and much, much more content made by AI. What goes out: your data, your words, your images. This is the gate where surveillance happens. Once you're through the entrance, there are more gates inside, for what you can do with others and what you can exchange. But it all starts with these four.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Gates give us control. They let us prevent entrances, interactions and transactions we don't want. And the first control we need is self-control: the gates we set for ourselves on what reaches us and what leaves us. Right now, most of those gates are set by platforms and their algorithms. But gates have a dark side. A gate that checks who you are can also watch who you are. That's the tension between safety and surveillance, between control and privacy. The question is whether gates are built to watch us or to protect us. Here's the way through. A good gate checks a claim, not a person. Are you a member? Are you over 18? Are you a real human? The aim is to answer yes without revealing your name, your history or your location. A bad gate demands your identity because that's easier to build. If we get gating right, we get control without surveillance. In the Desirable Properties, gates touch authentication and accountability, participant agency, and data sovereignty and privacy. Did we get gates right? Is something missing? Does gating deserve its own property?

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Tell us: add your perspective, and sign in so the idea stays yours. And one more thing: if you're building something good, now is the time to build. It is really go time. I can't say that enough. Carve out a few hours every week to build. Prepare now, build good, do it now. That's super important from my perspective at this moment.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: So, I would love to hear your questions and reactions. Is there anyone who would like to jump in? What's your experience with gates? What do you think about our treatment of gates in the book? And let me know if you're okay with your thoughts being put on video. Anyone? Hey, Rick. Do you all see the connection between gates and what we're doing with the Desirable Properties?

turns.speaker: Speaker unclear (participant A)
turns.text: Absolutely. The biggest thing seems to be agency. Do people even know that they're walking through a gate? What I really liked was the very beginning, how you're using it as a metaphor so people understand that they're entering a different environment the moment they start engaging with technology. I think that's extremely important: how we engage with information systems with our data, data sovereignty again, something we are constantly thinking about. And what you're able to leave with, what stays and what goes, even the record that you went through a gate in the first place, is all extremely important for the collective. I think the Desirable Properties cover what's happening on one side of the gate and how you can get to the other side, and there are some aspects about what you can take with you once you've crossed through. So at least in this first version, the Desirable Properties are addressing some of what gates can be established with respect to the internet, to information, and to how people engage technology.

turns.speaker: Speaker unclear (participant A)
turns.text: At a high level, some of these things are being addressed without selecting a specific DP or a specific attribute within a DP. And how we're coming together as a community to establish what those gates are and how they can function, even posing the question, is very healthy for a group to be doing. So yes, I see the connection, and I think it's a great topic and concept to be walking with.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Awesome. Thank you for that commentary. Are you comfortable with that potentially being used?

turns.speaker: Speaker unclear (participant A)
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, we can say that.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Okay. Awesome.

turns.speaker: Speaker unclear (participant B)
turns.text: What I think about is when I'm trying to enter certain spaces, personal or related to work, a pop-up window comes in and you have to type in your email address, and then I know I'm going to start getting all of these emails. To me, that's the kind of gate I come up against quite a bit, and I've found my own workaround: a fake email address. It's my email address and it literally says fake, so my real email isn't inundated with the aftermath. I'm putting it in to enter the space, but the space takes my email address for much broader purposes, often marketing or sharing my information. Or we have to select and unselect certain cookies, on every single page. What I liked about the possibility of the meta-layer is that we have control of that before we enter a space, without having to address it on every single site.

turns.speaker: Speaker unclear (participant B)
turns.text: I like the idea of what the metaweb makes possible: I'm in control, I decide, it's portable, it goes with me. It's not that on every page I enter I have to re-establish this; it's already with me. I don't know if that varies by state, country or website, but where I am, every time I go to a website I have to either adjust the cookies or enter my email address. So that's what I think about when you talk about gates: how the metaweb can mitigate those issues without us having to create a fake email. Those are our workarounds, but it can be possible without them.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Awesome. Thank you. Are you okay with us using that?

turns.speaker: Speaker unclear (participant B)
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: All right. Thank you. Rick, and then Salwa.

turns.speaker: Rick Botelho
turns.text: I really enjoyed the description you provided. The other issue is how aware people are of all of these gates, and I think most people are not very aware of them. As you were speaking, I was thinking of a four-column table about gates: your personal gate, encrypted; professional; the commons; and the corporate space. The reason I think it might be worthwhile, maybe asking AI to create a table to make those distinctions, is that most people aren't aware of how much they're giving away to the corporate space.

turns.speaker: Rick Botelho
turns.text: The expression is, there's no free lunch. People don't realize that when they're accessing these platforms, they're giving a lot away, and they're not even aware of how they're compromising their sovereignty. And lastly, I couldn't help but say this, Daveed, you might enjoy this one: you need to make a song about gates.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Of course. And a video as well.

turns.speaker: Rick Botelho
turns.text: And a video, yeah, to educate people about why gates are so important. Over, and you can use what I said.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Oh, thank you. Salwa had her hand up earlier. Are you still there?

turns.speaker: Salwa El Mais
turns.text: Yes. Thank you so much for the insights you have mentioned about the gates, and thanks to my colleagues. I think that gates are a very good idea, but I think there shouldn't be restrictions, or some restrictions shouldn't be imposed, so that most people who may use the metaweb won't be banned from something or have restrictions on something. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Thank you. Can we use your comment in a video?

turns.speaker: Salwa El Mais

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin

turns.text: Hi, Daveed. When you brought up gates, I don't know why, I instantly thought of gatekeepers. That's what came to mind. So I would like to emphasize that we're not gatekeepers in any way. Gates here mean, like you said, a doorway that we can pass through without discrimination, without divisions holding us back. That's all I wanted to emphasize.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Thank you. Can we use your comment?

turns.speaker: Laura Del Campo
turns.text: Of course.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Anyone else? Or Lela, is your hand back up?

turns.speaker: Leandra Preston
turns.text: Rick said something that made me think about my daughter, who is 13 now. Of course she's already got her email address, she's already interacting with a lot of spaces, she's very much online. If we don't understand the implications of sharing our information, it's hard to teach our kids to understand the implications of sharing theirs. And somebody who's not even an adult yet is already being manipulated with the information that companies and corporations have, or on social media. What does it mean to input your information? Now that she just turned 13, she has access to different sites and can make decisions about her own email address. What does that mean for somebody who's still a child? I feel like it must be adjusting the algorithm to target her, and how do I mitigate that? I think that's a really important topic for the next generation to understand.

turns.speaker: Salwa El Mais
turns.text: I totally agree with you.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Rick, you have your hand up?

turns.speaker: Rick Botelho
turns.text: Yeah, I'd like to build on that, because I think it's so critically important. In Australia, as you know, there are rules on kids' access up to the age of 16 [partly unclear]. The early tween and teen years are incredibly vulnerable, particularly for girls; see Jonathan Haidt's work on The Anxious Generation and all he's doing to protect children from these abuses. I think this is where parental supervision is needed. I work with a couple of young youth leaders [partly unclear], and I tell them, you need to get consent from your parents for what you're doing. Parental gates to protect children are incredibly important. And it's not easy, because I have a 12-year-old grandson, and boy, is it difficult even to understand the world he's getting exposed to in gaming. It's like abdicating parental responsibility, which is a real challenge: what rights do parents have over their children's development with social media? That's a huge area. Over and done.

turns.speaker: Leandra Preston
turns.text: And then there's the balance: she has friends who aren't allowed on social media at all, and what does that mean for their social interactions? There are so many issues that come into play when we're trying to protect children. Is the only solution forbidding them from it? We go through the algorithm together; we watch her social media together to see what her algorithm is doing and talk about it. But a lot of parents don't do that, or the answer is just not to allow the children on social media. I'm very pro-technology, like many of us, and I think about it as helping prepare her for the world she's growing into by being a critical viewer. But the limitation is my own knowledge: what do I not understand, what do I not know is happening? The implications are bigger than what I'm aware of. So it's a really important challenge to talk about and try to figure out.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Yeah, the internet and children is a huge topic, and a lot more needs to be done than has been done already. Michelle?

turns.speaker: Michelle Thuo
turns.text: When you mentioned gates, I was thinking about how we experience them in the physical world. A gate might be open, but if, for instance, there's no ramp, not everyone can get through it, even though it's open. I think the same applies to digital gates: even if a space is technically accessible, requirements around devices, connectivity or verification still create barriers for certain people. Perhaps the metaweb should also consider how to make these entry points accessible to people in different circumstances.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Thank you. Can we use that comment, by the way?

turns.speaker: Michelle Thuo
turns.text: Yes, sure.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin

DP, can you speak to what you've heard? I can't hear anything, but there's something happening in chat, so you can see how it would summarize.

turns.speaker: Rick Botelho
turns.text: I have a question for your agent, which ties in nicely: what are the desirable properties that parents need to assure that children benefit from the good of AI? How do you create a gated system so parents can feel confident that, when their children access different platforms or games, it's actually for the benefit of the child, as opposed to manipulating their attention for a commercial purpose? I don't know whether that's in your book, by the way. In your book, do you have something about the desirable properties for children?

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Well, the book didn't even have the concept of desirable properties at that point. But I believe it touches a little on it; there may be a section about how we might have a layer for young people, but I'm not totally sure.

turns.speaker: Rick Botelho
turns.text: There's something written about it. Well, you can use your AI to find out what there is. I may have to scoot; I'm getting a call. I'll come back if I can.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Sounds good. So DP said, answering Rick's question: “Rick, good question. I'm drawing on today's discussion here, not on a settled DP position. Properties that seem relevant for parents: verified, privacy-preserving age and guardian consent. That matches DP1 on authentication and DP4 on data sovereignty. Transparency about how algorithms treat children's attention: that is DP14 on trust and transparency.” Rick, are you seeing this in chat? I guess he stepped out.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: “Parents get visibility and control, which is DP2 on agency. Platforms are accountable to the children's benefit, not engagement. Gates should include: protect without excluding, as Michelle and Laura said.” And one other thing I wanted to bring up: gates is a concept that touches multiple DPs, and I'm wondering how we might incorporate it in the book, maybe as an unofficial part of the book, sections or specific chapters on things like gates, or sub-chapters. I'm not totally sure, but I wanted to throw that out to you all. We have a main book, the chapters of the DPs. Wouldn't it also be worthwhile to have another section of the book, unofficial or not, that allows for a chapter on gates, a chapter on some other thing, like a bridge or a smart tag? What do you all think?

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: If anyone has thoughts about that, you can bring them up at any point. I'm going to go back to the presentation, and we'll go through the results from last time. Thank you for all that input; that was amazing. We're going to talk about the vote and the process. What happened? What's the published record and the tally? What did we learn? Where did the process clarify choices, where did it create friction, and what would we want to change? We'll separate the outcome of this vote from proposals for the next one. The first ballot results: voting ended November 22nd at 8 p.m. Pacific. 24 people voted. I am so happy about that. 14 of the 15 questions are decided, published on the 16 November session page and also on the new session page we're building for today and the next week. To decide today: question 5, quorum, is a tie. A minimum of 20 votes and 25% of the voting body each got six votes.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: We'll talk more about that later. What rules governed this vote? You had to be signed in, one vote per account, and votes could change until closing. Most votes wins; a yes-or-no question needs more yeses than noes. Abstentions did not count at all. We didn't have any quorum rule; we're in bootstrap mode, so we may have a quorum in the future. That's something we need to decide. The results: on the pilot, 20 to 1 said yes for the next four weeks, so let's pilot this voting process and see how far it gets us. The approval rule: 50% keeps an item open, 60% or more passes it. That won with 11 votes; consent-based got six, more than 50% got three, 60% got three. Quorum: there was a tie, like we said, six votes for 25% of the voting body and six for no quorum [the published tally: a minimum of 20 votes 6, 25% of the voting body 6, no quorum 5]. Does anyone want to speak to their thoughts on this?

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: With 25% of the voting body: I don't know exactly how many people, but I think there are probably a hundred and something people who were either a contributor or a co-editor. We had 24 votes, so we're very close to 25% of the voting body. Do we want to make that a hard-and-fast rule? Anyone have thoughts about that? We're at a tie, so let's get some more input.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Would people be willing to consent to no quorum for the next four weeks? Or is there someone who would like to veto that? So it sounds like people are okay with no quorum, that they would consent to that. Is there anyone who wants to speak in favor of either no quorum or 25% of the voting body? Joel, hi Joel.

turns.speaker: Joel Okomoli
turns.text: Hi Daveed. I think 25% is fair. When it comes to quorum, it's about people's expressions, about feelings, about how people look at it. I hope you can hear me well.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Joel Okomoli
turns.text: The vote gives direction on the way we need to move forward. If we do not set a threshold on this, then we are moving in the wilderness. I would like to stand by 25%, because that gives, not clear consensus, but considerable consensus, a good above-average.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Thank you for that input. Maybe we could think about it as 25% of the active voting body, because there are people who have contributed but are not really active: not coming to meetings or paying attention to what's happening with the project. They made a contribution a while back; maybe I sent them an email and translated their response into a proposal. So let me look into that and get a sense of what the active voting body is, and I'll bring that back. I'll have it on the session page. The session page is the page we use for a given session; today's runs through the next week. We put the potential ballot items on it, refine them there, make comments, and then we do the vote there. I'll make sure this ends up on the session page for this week.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: More results. Co-editors: up to three seats, two approvals needed, 20 to 2. People are agreeing quite a bit on these. Review decisions: a decline keeps the current rule, so a decline will not kill a proposal, but you need two approvals to push it forward. Title changes: 75% of authors and co-editors, then the steering committee or council. I believe this is across the board: if someone wants to change a title, 75% of all the chapter's co-editors and authors would need to agree. That's a high threshold, but that's what 16 people said, so we're going to go with it. Joining the role: a co-editor agreement, yes, most people thought so. Vetting: a questionnaire screened against published criteria; more than half the people want that as well.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Should we elect a council to screen ballot readiness? Most people said yes. An interim council of five: yes. I think we just need to confirm: Lela and Renad said they were in, and Phahsa said he was in. There was one other person, Michelle. Michelle, are you okay with being on an interim council that would determine whether proposals can move forward, and at the same time, over the next several months, prepare us for voting in a non-interim council? Michelle, are you still there? Can someone look in participants and see if Michelle is here?

turns.speaker: Saramiris
turns.text: It says she's still here.

turns.speaker: Leandra Preston
turns.text: It looked like she unmuted. Maybe we just can't hear her for some reason.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Michelle, could you put a note in chat and let us know if you're trying to speak and we're not hearing you?

turns.speaker: Renad Baomar
turns.text: Maybe her internet connection.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Yeah, probably. So anyway, everybody said yes to an interim council. The scope: people liked it being the Meta-Layer Initiative, so the DPs plus the wider Meta-Layer Initiative, which would include the Metaweb Academy. That's great.

turns.speaker: Phahsa
turns.text: I just want to say, with the Meta-Layer Initiative and the Metaweb Academy, I don't think there was a clear roadmap as to what would be entailed in that piece.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Okay, I'll speak to it. In the near to medium term the Meta-Layer Initiative will be mainly focused on the DPs, and the Metaweb Academy is the other focus, around the certification program. Those will be the two main focuses of the Meta-Layer Initiative, unless the council decides it wants another focus.

turns.speaker: Phahsa
turns.text: That would be amazing to see.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Thanks for the question. Accountability: we need published screening criteria, and written reasons for holding items back. That was 21 to 2. We're getting a lot of agreement on these. The first cycle, going over what happened: we did the meeting, then a draft and a 24-hour review window, November 17 through 18, with a 12-hour notice that it was opening.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Something's missing, though; I remember something else we decided that we haven't spoken about. Oh, I said that because a 48-hour review period was chosen in the voting, and 72 hours for voting: people would love to have 72 hours for voting. Then we did the voting period. We didn't have council screening, because we didn't have a council yet. Today is November 23rd; we tallied the votes and published the ballot results. We still need to determine what to do with the quorum tie; maybe we'll put that into this week's record. So what should we improve? What do you all think? Did the draft faithfully capture the options, objections and unresolved questions? Did people know when to review and vote? Could they participate easily? How was the process? Was it easy for you?

turns.speaker: Leandra Preston
turns.text: I thought it was very easy and explainable, and the heads-up and reminder were helpful.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Awesome. The header still says voting: how do we keep status, outcomes and applied decisions in sync? I'll look into that; we can take care of it with code. Anyone else have anything about the process before we move on? Or should I assume it went pretty well? Let's move into the next week and continue evaluating it. Is that where you all are?

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Okay. Reviewing the next vote: which questions are settled, and which need clarification or new proposals? The main one is the quorum. We'll define the choices: state the problem, distinct options, consequences, any reasonable alternatives. And we can check readiness: what evidence or correction is needed before a question is ready for the ballot.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Next questions. Participation: who may vote, how eligibility is checked and how access barriers are handled. The thing I know we need to deal with at some point is making sure people don't have multiple accounts; at this point that is not in place, but it probably should be done soon. I don't think it's an issue; I don't think anyone voted multiple times, and even if they had, it probably wouldn't have made much difference, except for the quorum vote, perhaps. But that's something I think we should deal with. The record: transcript, access and retention. Do people have any issues with the transcripts being put on the session page and retained? Is that a good thing? How do you all feel about that?

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Right now we're saving the transcript, and there will be a 48-hour period for people to give material corrections before any review or ballot begins. Then: ties, conflicting outcomes, implementation owners and reopening a decision. Once something has been decided, there are things we need to do to bring it into operation.

turns.speaker: Joel Okomoli
turns.text: I think there was a hand up, in the previous section.

turns.speaker: Laura Del Campo
turns.text: Oh, I raised my hand. I was just going to agree with that, because we don't want to repeat something we already went over, and archiving all of that, being able to see the transcript, would be great. I agree with it.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Awesome. Okay. Mike McGuire suggested daily sprints as a review cadence: more time overall, but each step is easier to take on. I'm not sure, because he's not here to fully explain it, and I would love for Mike to explain it. So if we can put a note in here to get his input, that would be great, and hopefully we can get that through this next session cycle. Screening was skipped on this ballot, but now, assuming Michelle is okay, we have an interim council that will make that decision this week.

turns.text: There's a comment in the chat; I think she's in. Apparently her mic is off; I think she has a problem with the mic. If you scroll up a bit in the chat, you'll see her response.

turns.speaker: Joel Okomoli
turns.text: I think the interim council. When we were discussing the interim council, you asked whether she's in or not, and she answered in the chat.

turns.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
turns.text: Okay, great, perfect. So we have an interim council now. Awesome. I had a session with Markabadi, who's come to the last several meetings, and this is open to you all as well. He felt the process was a little challenging to jump right into. We had a session, I recorded the whole thing, and then we worked with DP to implement a number of things you may have seen, mostly around the look and format of the session page. I think they were really helpful; in my mind, the page improved a lot from the first iteration to this one. We have a record of that call in what I'm calling a landing pad. I think of the session pages as landing pads too: like a landing page, but it allows interaction and may have some personalization; it's something you want to interact with. So I created a landing pad for my conversation with Markabadi, which you can all review. turns.text: Everything that happened with this last vote is available from here, from the drafting process to the ballot to the results. turns.text: how can we make this clear, the voting-open status wasn't showing correctly before, breadcrumbs. Those were obvious improvements, so we went ahead and built them.
